High school head start

Earn college credit in high school without wasting courses

You can make progress toward college before high school ends. The useful head start is a course your future degree can use, at a price your family understands. Start with one good choice, then build from there.

Build my course collection

1. Decide what you want the course to count toward

A course can help with a high-school requirement, a future college degree, or both. Those are separate decisions. Your high school or homeschool program determines the high-school side; the college awarding your future degree decides which college requirements it accepts.

Choose a likely school and degree if you have one. If you are exploring, save a few course options and compare their fit across supported degree plans before buying. For example, an introductory business course that becomes an elective at one college might fill a named requirement at another. The course title alone cannot tell you that.

2. Check the local dual-enrollment option first

A local college partnership may cost less than a course you buy yourself. Ask your school counselor for the participating colleges, available subjects, enrollment dates and approval process. Include homeschool or private-school arrangements when those apply to you.

Florida provides one specific example. Its dual-enrollment program includes eligible students in grades 6–12 and home education. College readiness and articulation requirements apply, with separate home-education provisions. State law exempts eligible dual-enrollment students from registration, tuition and laboratory fees and addresses free instructional materials. That does not make every independently purchased online course part of the funded program.

Use the rules for your own state and school. Check transportation, scheduling and any remaining expenses alongside tuition. A genuinely useful course with funded tuition can be a better first choice than a paid subscription.

3. Know which kind of academic record you will earn

University coursework and ACE-recommended courses offer different routes. Both can be useful, but neither guarantees a place in every degree. Keep the original provider, course code and completion date in your course collection.

Save the original course identifier and completion date as well as the title. A completed row in your collection is not yet a degree award. Keep the receiving college’s decision alongside that row when it arrives. If you change majors, reuse the original record to compare alternatives instead of retaking it without checking.

Two accessible options, checked November 27, 2026. College and high-school acceptance remain separate.
OptionAccess and academic recordWhat to settle first
ASU Universal LearnerNo minimum age; eligible completed coursework can be added to an official ASU transcript after optional credit purchaseParent consent and identity steps, assessment requirements, high-school treatment and receiving-degree fit
SophiaIts official guidance allows learners as young as 13; courses carry ACE credit recommendations for receiving colleges to evaluateThe exact course/version accepted by your target college, high-school treatment and current membership terms

4. Follow the student and parent enrollment steps

ASU has a registration route for high-school learners and additional parental-consent steps for those under 18. Its identity rules permit a birth certificate to begin a course for an under-18 learner, but a proctored exam requires government-issued identification. Check the selected course before assuming the same documents work for every assessment.

ASU currently charges $25 to enroll and an optional $400 to add eligible completed coursework to its transcript. The credit-purchase choice lasts one year after completion; official transcript ordering can add a separate charge. High-school credit is still determined separately. For Sophia, use the provider’s current enrollment and identity instructions rather than assuming ASU’s consent process applies there too.

5. Keep college application status on your checklist

College credit earned during high school does not automatically make you a transfer applicant. ASU expressly treats learners taking college courses while still in high school as first-year applicants. It defines transfer applicants using at least 12 transferable credits completed after high school.

Other colleges set their own application categories and scholarship rules. Record when you will graduate and when each college course will be completed. Check the target school’s first-year rules before taking additional courses after graduation, particularly if you want the traditional campus experience. This is an admission decision, separate from how much credit the school applies.

6. Make a small plan you can actually finish

Start with one course that fits your preparation, school schedule and likely degree. Leave room for assignments, grading and transcript delivery. Flexible enrollment does not mean every course can produce a transcript immediately.

Your first checklist can be short: choose the requirement, confirm the high-school arrangement when needed, compare the full cost, complete any consent and identity steps, and save the original record. Mark a course complete only after you finish it; record the receiving college’s award separately. Add the next course when this process feels manageable.

Before you pay

Know the course, the requirement it is meant to fill, who issues the academic record and which costs your family will actually cover.

About this research

DegreeSteps editorial team · Degree planning and transfer-credit research

We explain educational choices using university catalogs, receiving-school course agreements, provider guidance, and the same researched degree models used by DegreeSteps. Our articles distinguish proposed coursework, original learning records, and individual university awards. Worked examples identify their program, format, units, and relevant dates. Founder stories are attributed as reported experience, without invented transcripts, savings totals, or reviewer credentials.
